summary: Deferasirox is an orally active, tridentate iron chelator selective for ferric iron (Fe3+), indicated for chronic iron overload due to blood transfusions in patients 2 years and older, and for chronic iron overload in non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia (NTDT) syndromes in patients 10 years and older meeting liver iron concentration and ferritin thresholds. Two molecules bind one iron atom (2:1) and the complex is excreted predominantly in the feces. It carries a boxed warning for renal failure, hepatic failure and gastrointestinal hemorrhage, all of which can be fatal, so baseline and ongoing monitoring of renal function, liver function, blood counts, ferritin, hearing and vision is essential. It is contraindicated when eGFR is below 40 mL/min/1.73m2, in poor performance status, high-risk MDS, advanced malignancy and platelet counts below 50 x 10^9/L.
indications: Treatment of chronic iron overload due to blood transfusions (transfusional hemosiderosis) in patients 2 years of age and older

Treatment of chronic iron overload in patients 10 years of age and older with non-transfusion-dependent thalassemia (NTDT) syndromes, with liver iron concentration of at least 5 mg Fe/g dry weight and serum ferritin greater than 300 mcg/L

moa: Deferasirox is an orally active chelator selective for iron in the ferric (Fe3+) state. It is a tridentate ligand that binds iron with high affinity in a 2:1 (ligand:iron) ratio, forming a stable complex that is excreted predominantly in the feces, thereby reducing tissue iron burden. It has very low affinity for zinc and copper, although variable decreases in these trace metals can occur.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to deferasirox or any component
relative: Pre-existing renal impairment (reduce starting dose, monitor closely)
Elderly and pediatric patients (age-related toxicity risk)

preg: There are no adequate human data. In animals, deferasirox caused decreased offspring viability and increased renal anomalies in male offspring at or below the recommended human dose on a mg/m2 basis. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Deferasirox may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives; advise an additional or alternative non-hormonal method.
lact: Deferasirox is excreted in the milk of lactating animals; effects on the breastfed infant and milk production are unknown. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment.
renal: Deferasirox can cause acute kidney injury, including acute renal failure requiring dialysis, and renal tubular toxicity including Fanconi syndrome. It is contraindicated when eGFR is below 40 mL/min/1.73m2. Measure serum creatinine in duplicate before starting, monitor renal function at least monthly (weekly for the first month in high-risk patients), reduce the starting dose in pre-existing renal disease, and reduce dose or interrupt therapy for renal toxicity.
hepatic: Deferasirox can cause hepatic injury including hepatic failure and death. Measure serum transaminases and bilirubin in all patients before treatment, every 2 weeks during the first month, and at least monthly thereafter. Reduce the dose or interrupt therapy for severe or persistent elevations in liver tests or other evidence of significant hepatic injury.

major: Aluminum-containing antacids - do not take concomitantly
Strong UGT inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, phenobarbital, ritonavir) - may decrease deferasirox exposure and efficacy
Other nephrotoxic or ulcerogenic/hemorrhagic drugs (e.g. NSAIDs, corticosteroids, oral bisphosphonates, anticoagulants) - increased risk of GI bleeding/renal injury
moderate: CYP3A4 substrates - deferasirox induces CYP3A4 and may reduce their concentrations (e.g. cyclosporine, simvastatin, hormonal contraceptives) - monitor effectiveness
Repaglinide (CYP2C8 substrate) - increased exposure; consider repaglinide dose reduction and monitor blood glucose
Theophylline (CYP1A2 substrate) - increased levels; avoid concomitant use
Busulfan - increased exposure; monitor levels for dose adjustment
minor: Bile acid sequestrants (e.g. cholestyramine) - may reduce deferasirox exposure
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach or with a light meal; a high-fat meal increases absorption of some formulations - keep the regimen consistent.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol, which adds to the risk of gastric irritation, GI ulceration/bleeding and hepatic injury.
interactions.diagnostics: Expect rises in serum creatinine and urinary protein; monitor ferritin and liver iron concentration to guide dosing.

serious: Acute kidney injury / acute renal failure and renal tubular toxicity (Fanconi syndrome)
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage, ulceration and irritation (fatal cases reported)
Bone marrow suppression - neutropenia, agranulocytosis, worsening anemia, thrombocytopenia
Severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS)
Hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis and angioedema

monitoring: Serum creatinine in duplicate at baseline, then at least monthly (weekly for the first month in high-risk patients); calculate eGFR
Serum transaminases and bilirubin before treatment, every 2 weeks for the first month, then monthly
Complete blood count, particularly in patients with pre-existing cytopenias
Serum ferritin monthly and periodic liver iron concentration to guide dosing
Auditory (audiometry) and ophthalmologic testing before and periodically during treatment
Signs of GI bleeding, rash and hypersensitivity
counsel: Take once a day at the same time, on an empty stomach or with a light meal
Do not take aluminum-containing antacids with this medicine
Report decreased urination, swelling, severe abdominal pain, vomiting blood or black stools, yellowing of the skin or eyes
Report any rash, hearing changes or vision changes promptly
Keep all appointments for blood, urine, hearing and eye tests
Use a non-hormonal back-up contraceptive method as this drug can reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy
pk: Net iron excretion begins with regular daily dosing; ferritin trends guide response over weeks
Plasma concentrations peak within a few hours of oral dosing
Once-daily dosing maintains iron-chelating effect; iron excretion is predominantly fecal
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions 15-30 C permitted; protect from moisture
pearls: Boxed warning: renal failure, hepatic failure and GI hemorrhage - all potentially fatal
Contraindicated when eGFR is below 40 mL/min/1.73m2 and when platelets are below 50 x 10^9/L
Measure serum creatinine in duplicate at baseline and monitor renal function at least monthly
Induces CYP3A4 - can lower levels of cyclosporine, statins and hormonal contraceptives; advise non-hormonal contraception
Avoid concomitant aluminum-containing antacids and limit drugs with ulcerogenic/hemorrhagic potential
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is nearly time for the next day's dose, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the usual time. Do not take two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
overdose: Reported overdoses (2-3 times the prescribed dose for several weeks) have caused hepatitis and, in a pediatric case, acute renal failure requiring hemofiltration and acute liver injury, both reversible with intensive support. A single erroneous 90 mg/kg dose led to reversible Fanconi syndrome. Early signs include abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting. There is no specific antidote; manage with induction of vomiting or gastric lavage and symptomatic supportive care, including renal and hepatic support.
